interpretation: Most exact-point alternative-seagrass occupancy one year after Thalassia loss represents persistence of at least one alternative species already co-occurring at that same meter mark. This supports selective focal-species dropout from pre-existing mixed patches as a common route to apparent community replacement, rather than entirely de novo colonization after focal loss.
claim_boundary: Post-hoc exploratory community ecology; endpoint frozen before source-target alternative-species overlap was opened.
Persistence of a co-occurring alternative species is consistent with species-specific dropout from a mixed patch, not proof of facilitation, competition, or causal displacement.
Target-only appearance need not equal biological colonization because detection can vary between annual visits.
Segment-specific and taxon-specific fractions are descriptive secondary results.
The result concerns point-scale community-state turnover and does not establish equivalent ecosystem function after Thalassia loss.
